t: The Sámi are the Indigenous people of Sápmi, speaking about ten related Uralic languages, and have lived in the far north of Europe since the Bronze Age or early Iron Age.
For most of their history they lived by fishing, hunting, trapping and trade; large-scale reindeer herding grew from about 1500, and today about one Sámi in ten is connected to it.
Taxation, forced conversion, closed borders and assimilation policies bore down on them for centuries; since the 1970s Sámi parliaments, a flag, an anthem and a national day have marked a revival.
dyk: All modern versions of the board game hnefatafl, usually sold as a Viking game, are based on the Sámi game tablut, the only tafl game whose rules survived relatively intact.
ev: Tacitus describes the Fenni, probably the first historical mention of the Sámi
The Black Death reaches northern Norway; Sámi later settle the abandoned farms, and the Sea Sámi way of life takes shape
Wild reindeer decline under hunting driven by taxes, and reindeer herding begins to grow
The Lapp Codicil to the Strömstad Treaty sets out how Sámi may use the land across the Swedish–Norwegian border
Sámi angered by religious persecution and Norwegianisation rise in the Kautokeino Rebellion
The first Sámi congress meets in Trondheim, bringing Norwegian and Swedish Sámi together
The Alta hydro-electric controversy brings Sámi rights onto the political agenda
The first Sámi Parliament in Norway is elected, after Finland’s of 1973 and before Sweden’s of 1993

f.homeland: Sápmi, formerly called Lapland: northern Norway, Sweden and Finland and the Kola Peninsula of Russia; centres include Guovdageaidnu (Kautokeino), Kárášjohka (Karasjok), Inari, Jokkmokk and Lovozero; once also southern Finland
f.period: Arrived in Sápmi in the Bronze Age or early Iron Age (2nd–1st millennia BCE); the Sámi proto-language formed c. 2,000–2,500 years ago (Ante Aikio); reindeer nomadism from c. 1500 CE; ruled by the surrounding states from the 15th century; a living people
f.known: the Sámi languages of the Uralic family; reindeer herding in siidas; Sea Sámi fishing; joik; duodji crafts and gákti clothing; the noaidi and painted drums; the board game tablut; the Sámi Parliaments, flag and National Day
f.sources: Roman and Greek mentions of the Fenni and Phinnoi; the account of Ohthere to King Alfred; Norse sagas; Johannes Schefferus’s Lapponia (1673); archaeology and place names; linguistics; genetic studies; Sámi joik, oral tradition and writing
